entries.7a2c1e87e9e574ad0f16d0d452c25dfc3e604678: <div sID="gen20096" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Amos.2" sID="Amos.2"/> <div eID="gen20096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20097" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20098" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. God, by the prophet, proceeds in a like controversy with Moab as before with other nations, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.1-Amos.2.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He shows what quarrel he had with Judah, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.4-Amos.2.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. III. He at length begins his charge against Israel, to which all that goes before is but an introduction. Observe, 1. The sins they are charged with—injustice, oppression, whoredom, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.6-Amos.2.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. 2. The aggravations of those sins—the temporal and spiritual mercies God had bestowed upon them, for which they had made him such ungrateful returns, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.9-Amos.2.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. 3. God's complaint of them for their sins (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.13">ver. 13</reference>) and his threatenings of their ruin, and their utter inability to prevent it, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.14-Amos.2.16">ver. 14-16</reference>.
entries.34c0a7386ec78da837295f66d2433cbdc1e96617: <div eID="gen20098" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20097" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Moab and of Judah; The Judgment of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20099" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away <hi type="italic">the punishment</hi> thereof; because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime: <hi type="super">2</hi> But I will send a fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the palaces of Kerioth: and Moab shall die with tumult, with shouting, <hi type="italic">and</hi> with the sound of the trumpet: <hi type="super">3</hi> And I will cut off the judge from the midst thereof, and will slay all the princes thereof with him, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">4</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; For three transgressions of Judah, and for four, I will not turn away <hi type="italic">the punishment</hi> thereof; because they have despised the law of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and have not kept his commandments, and their lies caused them to err, after the which their fathers have walked: <hi type="super">5</hi> But I will send a fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away <hi type="italic">the punishment</hi> thereof; because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes; <hi type="super">7</hi> That pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor, and turn aside the way of the meek: and a man and his father will go in unto the <hi type="italic">same</hi> maid, to profane my holy name: <hi type="super">8</hi> And they lay <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, and they drink the wine of the condemned <hi type="italic">in</hi> the house of their god. <div eID="gen20099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20100" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The judgment of Moab, another of the nations that bordered upon Israel. They are reckoned with and shall be punished <hi type="italic">for three transgressions and for four,</hi> as those before. Now, 1. Moab's fourth transgression, as theirs who were before set to the bar, was cruelty. The instance given refers not to the people of God, but to a heathen like themselves: The king of Moab <hi type="italic">burnt the bones of the king of Edom into lime.</hi> We find there was war between the Edomites and the Moabites, in which the king of Moab, in distress and rage, offered his own son for a burnt-offering, to appease his deity, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.26-2Kgs.3.27">2 Kings iii. 26, 27</reference>. And it should seem that afterwards he, or some of his successors, in revenge upon the Edomites for bringing him to that extremity, having an advantage against the <hi type="italic">king of Edom,</hi> seized him alive and burnt him to ashes, or slew him and burnt his body, or dug up the bones of their dead king, of that particularly who had so straitened him, and, in token of his rage and fury, <hi type="italic">burnt them to lime.</hi> and perhaps made use of the powder of his bones for the white-washing of the walls and ceilings of his palace, that he might please himself with the sight of that monument of his revenge. <hi type="italic">Est vindicta bonum vita jucundius ipsa—Revenge is sweeter than life itself.</hi> It is barbarous to abuse human bodies, for we ourselves also are <hi type="italic">in the body;</hi> it is senseless to abuse dead bodies, nay, it is impious, for we believe and look for their resurrection; and to abuse the dead bodies of kings (whose persons and names ought to be in a particular manner respected and had in veneration) is an affront to majesty; it is an argument of a base spirit for those to trample upon a dead lion who, were he alive, would tremble before him. 2. Moab's doom for this transgression is, (1.) A judgment of death. Those that deal cruelly shall be cruelly dealt with (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Moab shall die;</hi> the Moabites shall be cut off with the sword of war, which kills <hi type="italic">with tumult, with shouting, and with sound of trumpet,</hi> circumstances that make it so much the more terrible, as the lion's roaring aggravates his tearing. <hi type="italic">Every battle of the warrior is with confused noise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.5">Isa. ix. 5</reference>. (2.) It is a judgment upon their judge, who had passed the sentence upon the bones of the king of Edom that they should be burnt to lime: <hi type="italic">I will cut him off,</hi> says God (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.3">v. 3</reference>); he shall know there is a judge that is higher than he. The king, the chief judge, and all the inferior judges and princes, shall be cut off together. If the people sometimes suffer for the sin of their princes, yet the princes themselves shall not escape, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.47">Jer. xlviii. 47</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thus far is the judgment of Moab.</hi> <div eID="gen20100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20101" type="x-p"/> II. Judah also is a near neighbour to Israel, and therefore, now that justice is riding the circuit, that shall not be passed by; that nation has made itself like the heathen and mingled with them, and therefore the indictment here runs against them in the same form in which it had run against all the rest: <hi type="italic">For these transgressions of Judah, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof;</hi> their sins are as many as the sins of other nations, and we find them huddled up with them in the same character, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.26">Jer. ix. 26</reference>, "As for <hi type="italic">Egypt, and Judah, and Edom,</hi> jumble them together; they are all alike;" the sentence here also is the same (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will send a fire upon Judah,</hi> though it is the land where God is known, and it shall <hi type="italic">devour the palaces of Jerusalem,</hi> though it is the holy city, and God has formerly been <hi type="italic">known in its palaces for a refuge,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.48.3">Ps. xlviii. 3</reference>. But the sin here charged upon Judah is different from all the rest. The other nations were reckoned with for injuries done to men, but Judah is reckoned with for indignities done to God, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.4">v. 4</reference>. 1. They put contempt upon his statutes and persisted in disobedience to them: <hi type="italic">They have despised the law of the Lord,</hi> as if it were not worth taking notice of, nor had any thing in it valuable; and herein they despised the wisdom, justice, and goodness, as well as the authority and sovereignty, of the Lawmaker; this they did, in effect, when they <hi type="italic">kept not his commandments,</hi> made no conscience of them, took no care about them. 2. They put honour upon his rivals, their idols, here called <hi type="italic">their lies</hi> which caused <hi type="italic">them to err;</hi> for <hi type="italic">an image is a teacher of lies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.18">Hab. ii. 18</reference>. And those that are led away into the error of idolatry are by that led into a multitude of other errors, <hi type="italic">Uno dato absurdo mille sequuntur—One absurdity draws after it a thousand.</hi> God is an infinite eternal Spirit; but, when the <hi type="italic">truth of God</hi> is by idolatry <hi type="italic">changed into a lie,</hi> all his other truths are in danger of being so changed likewise; thus their idols caused them to err, and God justly gave them up to strong delusions; nor was it any excuse for their sin that they were lies <hi type="italic">after which their father walked,</hi> for they should rather have taken warning than taken pattern by those that perished with these <hi type="italic">lies in their right hand.</hi> <div eID="gen20101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20102" type="x-p"/> III. We now at length come to <hi type="italic">the words</hi> which <hi type="italic">Amos saw concerning Israel.</hi> The reproofs and threatenings having walked the round, here they centre, here they settle. He begins with them as with the rest: <hi type="italic">For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof;</hi> if all these nations must be punished for their iniquities, shall Israel go unpunished? Observe here what their sins were, for which God would reckon with them. 1. Perverting justice. This was the sin of those who were entrusted with the administration of justice, the judges and magistrates, and all parties concerned. They made nothing of selling a righteous man, and his righteous cause when it came to be tried before them, for a piece of silver; sentence was passed, not according to the merits of the cause, but the bribe always turned the scale, and judgment was set to sale by auction to the highest bidder. They would sell the life and livelihood of a <hi type="italic">poor</hi> man <hi type="italic">for a pair of shoes,</hi> for the least advantage to themselves that could be proposed to them; give them but a <hi type="italic">pair of shoes,</hi> and the cause of a poor man, who could not give them as much as that, should be betrayed, and left at the mercy of those that will have no mercy. They will rather play at small game that sit out. <hi type="italic">For a piece of bread such a man will transgress.</hi> Note, Those who will wrong their consciences for any thing will come at length to do it for next to nothing; those who begin to sell justice for silver will in time be so sordid as to see it <hi type="italic">for a pair of shoes,</hi> for a pair of old shoes. 2. Oppressing the poor, and seeking to benefit themselves by doing them a mischief: <hi type="italic">They pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor;</hi> they swallow up the poor with the utmost greediness, and make a prey of those that are in sorrow with dust on their heads, poor orphans that are in mourning for their parents; they catch at them to get their estates into their hands; they never rest till they have got the heads of the poor in the dust, to be trodden on. Or, <hi type="italic">They pant after the dust of the earth,</hi> that is, silver and gold, white and yellow dust; they covet it earnestly, and levy it <hi type="italic">upon the head of the poor</hi> by their unjust exactions. Note, Men's seeking to enrich themselves by the impoverishing of others is a transgression which God will not long <hi type="italic">turn away the punishment of.</hi> This is <hi type="italic">turning aside the way of the meek,</hi> contriving to do injury to those who, they know, are mild and patient and will bear injury. They invade their rights, break their measures, and obstruct the course of justice in favour of them, not suffering them to go on with their righteous cause; this is <hi type="italic">turning aside their way.</hi> Note, The more patiently men bear injuries that are done them the greater is the sin of those that injure them, and the more occasion they have to expect that God will give them redress, and take vengeance for them. I, <hi type="italic">as a deaf man, heard not,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">thou wilt hear.</hi> 3. Abominable uncleanness, even incest itself, such as it not named among the Gentiles, that <hi type="italic">a man should have his father's wife</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.1">1 Cor. v. 1</reference>), his father's concubine: <hi type="italic">A man and his father will go in unto the same young woman,</hi> as black an instance as any other of an unbounded promiscuous lust; and yet where the former iniquities of oppression and extortion are this also is found; for laws of modesty seldom hold those that have broken the bands of justice and <hi type="italic">cast away its cords</hi> from them. This wickedness is such a scandal to religion, and the profession of it, that those who are guilty of it are looked upon as designing thereby to <hi type="italic">profane God's holy name,</hi> and to render it odious among the heathen, as if he countenanced the villainies which those who pretend relation to him allow themselves in, and were altogether such a one as they. 4. Regaling themselves and yet pretending to honour their God with that which they had got by oppression and extortion, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.8">v. 8</reference>. They add idolatry to their injustice, and then think to atone for their injustice with their idolatry. (1.) They make merry with that which they have unjustly squeezed from the poor. They <hi type="italic">lay themselves down</hi> at ease, and in state, and stretch themselves upon <hi type="italic">clothes laid to pledge,</hi> which they ought to have restored the same night, according to the law, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.12-Deut.24.13">Deut. xxiv. 12, 13</reference>. And they <hi type="italic">drink the wine of the condemned,</hi> of such as they have fined and laid heavy mulcts upon, spending that in sensuality which they have got by injustice. (2.) They think to make atonement for this by feasting on the gains of oppression <hi type="italic">before their altars,</hi> and <hi type="italic">drinking this wine in the house of their God,</hi> in the temples where they worshipped their calves, as if they would make God a <hi type="italic">partner in their crimes</hi> by making him a <hi type="italic">partner of the profits</hi> of them—service good enough for false gods; but the true God will not thus be mocked; he has declared that he <hi type="italic">hates robbery for burnt-offerings,</hi> and cannot be served acceptably but with that which is got honestly.
entries.5e484494cc8bf51067721a6323ebfd5cebb24f8d: <div eID="gen20102" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Remonstrance with Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20103" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Yet destroyed I the Amorite before them, whose height <hi type="italic">was</hi> like the height of the cedars, and he <hi type="italic">was</hi> strong as the oaks; yet I destroyed his fruit from above, and his roots from beneath. <hi type="super">10</hi> Also I brought you up from the land of Egypt, and led you forty years through the wilderness, to possess the land of the Amorite. <hi type="super">11</hi> And I raised up of your sons for prophets, and of your young men for Nazarites. <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> not even thus, O ye children of Israel? saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">12</hi> But ye gave the Nazarites wine to drink; and commanded the prophets, saying, Prophesy not. <hi type="super">13</hi> Behold, I am pressed under you, as a cart is pressed <hi type="italic">that is</hi> full of sheaves. <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore the flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not strengthen his force, neither shall the mighty deliver himself: <hi type="super">15</hi> Neither shall he stand that handleth the bow; and <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> swift of foot shall not deliver <hi type="italic">himself:</hi> neither shall he that rideth the horse deliver himself. <hi type="super">16</hi> And <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> courageous among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen20103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20104" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God puts his people Israel in mind of the great things he has done for them, in putting them into possession of the land of Canaan, the greatest part of which these ten tribes now enjoyed, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.9-Amos.2.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Note, We need often to be reminded of the mercies we have received, which are the heaviest aggravations of the sins we have committed. God gives liberally, and upbraids us not with our meanness and unworthiness, and the disproportion between his gifts and our merits; but he justly upbraids us with our ingratitude, and ill requital of his favours, and tells us what he has done for us, to shame us for not rendering again according to the benefit done to us. "<hi type="italic">Son, remember;</hi> Israel, remember, 1. That God brought thee out of a house of bondage, rescued thee out of the <hi type="italic">land of Egypt,</hi> where thou wouldst otherwise have perished in slavery." 2. That he <hi type="italic">led thee forty years</hi> through a desert land, and fed thee in a <hi type="italic">wilderness,</hi> where thou wouldst otherwise have perished with hunger. Mercies to our ancestors were mercies to us, for, if they had been cut off, we should not have been. 3. That he made room for them in Canaan, by extirpating the natives by a series of wonders little inferior to those by which they were redeemed out of Egypt: <hi type="italic">I destroyed the Amorite before them,</hi> here put for all the devoted nations. Observe the magnificence of the enemies that stood in their way, which is taken notice of, that God may be the more magnified in the subduing of them. They were of great stature (<hi type="italic">whose height was like the height of the cedars</hi>) and the people of Israel were as shrubs to them; and they were also of great strength, not only tall, but well-set: <hi type="italic">He was strong as the oaks.</hi> Their kingdom was eminent among the nations, and over-topped all its neighbours. The supports and defences of it seemed impregnable; it was as fine as the stately cedar; it was as firm as the sturdy oak; yet, when God had a vine to plant there (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.8-Ps.80.9">Ps. lxxx. 8, 9</reference>), this Amorite was not only cut down, but plucked up: <hi type="italic">I destroyed his fruit from above and his roots from beneath,</hi> so that the Amorites were no more a nation, nor ever read of any more. Thus highly did God value Israel. He gave men <hi type="italic">for them and people for their life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 4</reference>. How ungrateful then were those who put such contempt upon him! 4. That he made them <hi type="italic">possess the land of the Amorite,</hi> not only put it into their hands, so that they became masters of it <hi type="italic">jure belli—by right of conquest,</hi> but gave them a better title to it, so that it became theirs by promise. <div eID="gen20104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20105" type="x-p"/> II. He likewise upbraids them with the spiritual privileges and advantages they enjoyed as a holy nation, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.11">v. 11</reference>. They had helps for their souls, which taught them how to make good use of their temporal enjoyments and were therefore more valuable. It is true the <hi type="italic">ten tribes</hi> had not God's temple, altar, and priesthood, and it was their own fault that they deserted them, and for that they might justly have been left in utter darkness; but God <hi type="italic">left not himself without witness,</hi> nor them without guides to show them the way. 1. They had prophets that were powerful instructors in piety, divinely inspired, and commissioned to make known the mind of God to them, to show them what is pleasing to God and what displeasing, to reprove them for their faults and warn them of their dangers, to direct them in their difficulties and comfort them in their troubles. God raised them up prophets, animated them for that work and employed them in it. He <hi type="italic">raised</hi> them <hi type="italic">up of their sons,</hi> from among themselves, as Moses and Christ were raised up <hi type="italic">from among their brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.18.15">Deut. xviii. 15</reference>. It was an honour put upon their nation, and upon their families, that they had children of their own to be God's messengers to them, of their own language, not strangers sent from another country, whom they might suspect to be prejudiced against them and their land, but those who, they knew, wished well to them. Note, Faithful ministers are great blessings to any people, and it is God that raises them up to be so, that they may justly be reckoned an honour to the families they are of. 2. They had Nazarites that were bright examples of piety: <hi type="italic">I raised up of your young men for Nazarites,</hi> men that bound themselves by a vow to God and his service, and, in pursuance of that, denied themselves many of the lawful delights of sense, as drinking wine and eating grapes. There were some of their young men that were in their prime for the enjoyment of the pleasures of this life and yet voluntarily abridged themselves of them; these God raised up by the power of his grace, to be <hi type="italic">monuments of his grace,</hi> to his glory, and to be his witnesses against the impieties of that degenerate age. Note, It is as great a blessing to any place to have eminent good Christians in it as to have eminent good ministers in it; for so they have examples to their rules. We must acknowledge that it bodes well to any people when God raises up numbers of hopeful young people among them, when he makes their young men Nazarites, devout, and conscientious, and mortified to the pleasures of sense; and those that are such Nazarites are <hi type="italic">purer than snow, whiter than milk;</hi> they are indeed the polite young men, for their <hi type="italic">polishing is of sapphires,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.7">Lam. iv. 7</reference>. Those that have such men, such young men, among them, have therein such an advantage, both for direction and encouragement, to be religious, as they will be called to an account for another day if they do not improve. Israel is here reckoned with, not only for the prophets, but for the Nazarites, raised up among them. Concerning the truth of this, he appeals to themselves: "<hi type="italic">Is it not even thus, O you children of Israel?</hi> Can you deny it? Have not you yourselves been sensible of the advantage you had by the prophets and Nazarites raised up among you?" Note, Sinners' own consciences will be witnesses for God that he has not been wanting to them in the means of grace, so that, if they perish, it is because they have been wanting to themselves in not improving those means. The men of Judah shall themselves <hi type="italic">judge between God and his vineyard,</hi> whether he could have done more for it, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.3-Isa.5.4">Isa. v. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen20105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20106" type="x-p"/> III. He charges them with the abuse of the means of grace they enjoyed, and the opposition they gave to God's designs in affording them those means, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.12">v. 12</reference>. They were so far from walking in the light that they rebelled against it, and did what they could to extinguish it, that it might not shine in their faces, to their conviction. 1. They did what they could to debauch good people, to draw them off from their seriousness in devotion and their strictness in conversation: <hi type="italic">You gave the Nazarites wine to drink,</hi> contrary to their vow, that, having broken it in that instance, they might not pretend to keep it in any other. Some they surprised, or allured into it, and <hi type="italic">with their much fair speech caused them to yield;</hi> others they forced and frightened into it, reproached and threatened them if they were more precise than their neighbours; and, by drawing them in to drink wine, they spoiled them for Nazarites. Note, Satan and his agents are very busy to corrupt the minds of young people that look heavenward; and many that we thought would have been Nazarites they have overcome by giving them wine to drink, by drawing them in to the love of mirth and pleasure, and drinking company. Multitudes of young men that bade fair for eminent professors of religion have <hi type="italic">erred through wine,</hi> and been undone for ever. And how do the factors for hell triumph in the debauching of a Nazarite! 2. They did what they could to silence good ministers, and to stop their mouths: "<hi type="italic">You commanded the prophets, saying, Prophesy not,</hi> and threatened them if they did prophesy (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.12">ch. vii. 12</reference>), as if God's messengers were bound to observe your orders, and might not deliver their errand unless you gave them leave, and so you not only <hi type="italic">received the grace of God,</hi> in raising up those prophets, <hi type="italic">in vain,</hi> but put the highest affront imaginable upon that God in whose name the prophets spoke." Note, Those have a great deal to answer for that cannot bear faithful preaching, and those much more that suppress it. <div eID="gen20106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20107" type="x-p"/> IV. He complains of the wrong they did him by their sins (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I am pressed under you,</hi> I am <hi type="italic">straitened</hi> by you, and can no longer bear it, and therefore <hi type="italic">I will ease myself of my adversaries,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Isa. i. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">I am pressed under you</hi> and the load of your sins <hi type="italic">as a cart is pressed that is full of sheaves,</hi> is loaded with corn, in the midst of the <hi type="italic">joy of harvest,</hi> as long as any will lie on." Note, The great God complains of sin, especially the sins of his professing people, as a burden to him. He is <hi type="italic">grieved with this generation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.10">Ps. xcv. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">is broken with their whorish heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.9">Ezek. vi. 9</reference>), a consideration which, if it make not the sinner's repentance very deep, will make his ruin very great. The great God that upholds the world, and never complains that his is pressed under the weight of it (he <hi type="italic">fainteth not, neither is weary</hi>), yet complains of the sins of Israel, yea, and of their hypocritical services too, that he is <hi type="italic">weary of bearing them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.14">Isa. i. 14</reference>. No wonder the <hi type="italic">creature groans being burdened</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.22">Rom. viii. 22</reference>), when the Creator says, <hi type="italic">I am pressed under them.</hi> <div eID="gen20107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20108" type="x-p"/> V. He threatens them with unavoidable ruin. And so some read, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.13">v. 13</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Behold I will press,</hi> or straiten, <hi type="italic">your place, as a cart full of sheaves presses;</hi> they shall be loaded with judgments till they shall sink under them, and shall make a noise, as a cart overloaded does." Those that will not submit to the convictions of the word, that will neither be won by that nor by the conversation of those about them, shall be made to sink under the weight of God's judgments. If God load us daily with his benefits, and we, notwithstanding that, load him with our sins, how can we expect any other than that he should load us with his judgments? And it is here threatened in the <reference osisRef="Amos.2.14-Amos.2.16">last three verses</reference> that, when God comes forth to contend with this provoking people, they shall not be able to stand before him, to flee from him, nor to make their part good with him; for when God judges he will overcome. Though his patience be tired out, his power is not, and so the sinner shall find, to his cost. When the Assyrian army comes to lay the country waste by sword and captivity none shall escape, but every one shall have his share in the common desolation. 1. It will be in vain to think of fleeing from the enemy that comes armed with a commission to make all desolate: <hi type="italic">The flight shall perish from the swift;</hi> those that have been famed for happy escapes and happy retreats shall now find their arts fail them; they shall have no time to flee, or shall find no way to take, or they shall have no strength or spirit to attempt it; they shall be at their wits' end, and then they are soon at their flight's end. Are they, as Asahel, as <hi type="italic">swift of foot as a wild roe?</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.18">2 Sam. ii. 18</reference>), yet, like him, they shall run the faster upon their own destruction: <hi type="italic">He that is swift of foot shall not deliver himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.2.15">v. 15</reference>. Or do they say (as those, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.16">Isa. xxx. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">We will flee upon horses,</hi> and <hi type="italic">we will ride upon the swift?</hi> Yet they shall be overtaken: <hi type="italic">Neither shall he that rides the horse deliver himself</hi> from his pursuers. <hi type="italic">A horse is a vain thing for safety.</hi> 2. It will be in vain to think of fighting it out. God is at war with them; and <hi type="italic">are they stronger than he?</hi> Is there any military force that can pretend to be a match for Omnipotence? No: <hi type="italic">The strong shall not strengthen his force.</hi> He that has a habit of strength shall not be able to exert it when he has occasion for it. And <hi type="italic">the mighty,</hi> whose should protect and deliver others, shall not be able to <hi type="italic">deliver himself,</hi> to deliver <hi type="italic">his soul</hi> (so the word is), shall not save his life. Let not the <hi type="italic">strong man</hi> then <hi type="italic">glory in his strength,</hi> nor trust in it, but <hi type="italic">strengthen himself in the Lord his God,</hi> for in him is <hi type="italic">everlasting strength.</hi> And, as the bodily strength shall fail, so shall the weapons of war. The armour as well as the arm shall become insufficient: <hi type="italic">Neither shall he stand that handles the bow,</hi> though he stand at a distance, but shall betake himself to flight, and not trust to his own bow to save him. Though the arm be ever so strong, and the armour ever so well fixed, neither will avail when the spirit fails (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that is courageous among the mighty,</hi> that used to look danger in the face, and not be dismayed at it, shall <hi type="italic">flee away naked in that day,</hi> not only disarmed, having thrown away his weapons both offensive and defensive, but plundered of his treasure, which he thought to carry away with him, and he shall think it as much as he could expect that he has <hi type="italic">his life for a prey.</hi> Thus when God pleases <hi type="italic">he takes away the heart of the chief of the people of the earth,</hi> and causes those who used to boast of their courage, and their daring enterprises in the field, to <hi type="italic">wander</hi> and sneak <hi type="italic">in a wilderness where there is no way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.24">Job xii. 24</reference>.  <chapter eID="Amos.2"/> <div eID="gen20108" type="x-p"/>

entries.e81e499c1f2a9a90ac0304d6505734c9cb88f18f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12522"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Amos.2.1-Amos.2.16">Am 2:1-16</reference>. Charges against Moab, Judah, and Lastly Israel, the Chief Subject of Amos' Prophecies.</title> <div sID="gen23038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12522"/><hi type="bold">1. burned ... bones of ... king of Edom into lime--</hi>When Jehoram of Israel, Jehoshaphat of Judah, and the king of Edom, combined against Mesha king of Moab, the latter failing in battle to break through to the king of Edom, took the oldest son of the latter and offered him as a burnt offering on the wall (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.27">2Ki 3:27</reference>) [Michaelis]. Thus, "king of Edom" is taken as the heir to the throne of Edom. But "his son" is rather the king of Moab's own son, whom the father offered to Molech [Josephus, Antiquities, 9.3]. Thus the reference here in Amos is not to that fact, but to the revenge which probably the king of Moab took on the king of Edom, when the forces of Israel and Judah had retired after their successful campaign against Moab, leaving Edom without allies. The Hebrew tradition is that Moab in revenge tore from their grave and burned the bones of the king of Edom, the ally of Jehoram and Jehoshaphat, who was already buried. Probably the "burning of the bones" means, "he burned the king of Edom alive, reducing his very bones to lime" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen23038" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e083ecf99aa61d69158a6b4c865d80c903de623: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12523"/><div sID="gen23039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12523"/><hi type="bold">2. Kirioth--</hi>the chief city of Moab, called also Kir-Moab (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Is 15:1</reference>). The form is plural here, as including both the acropolis and town itself (see <reference osisRef="Jer.48.24">Jr 48:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.41">41</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen23039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">die with tumult--</hi>that is, amid the tumult of battle (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.14">Ho 10:14</reference>). <div eID="gen23040" type="x-p"/>
entries.cba605709d997c098b3a6269bcb06007970b8d3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12524"/><div sID="gen23041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12524"/><hi type="bold">3. the judge--</hi>the chief magistrate, the supreme source of justice. "King" not being used, it seems likely a change of government had before this time substituted for kings, supreme judges. <div eID="gen23041" type="x-p"/>
entries.17ca3c5a6de27c6eba9ab08bef0ca4651b322dbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12525"/><div sID="gen23042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12525"/>4. From foreign kingdoms he passes to Judah and Israel, lest it should be said, he was strenuous in denouncing sins abroad, but connived at those of his own nation. Judah's guilt differs from that of all the others, in that it was directly against God, not merely against man. Also because Judah's sin was wilful and wittingly against light and knowledge.<div eID="gen23042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">law--</hi>the Mosaic code in general.<div eID="gen23043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commandments--</hi>or statutes, the ceremonies and civil laws.<div eID="gen23044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their lies--</hi>their lying idols (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">Psa 40:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.19">Jr 16:19</reference>), from which they drew false hopes. The order is to be observed. The Jews first cast off the divine law, then fall into lying errors; God thus visiting them with a righteous retribution (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.25">Ro 1:25</reference>, 26, 28; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11">2Th 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). The pretext of a good intention is hereby refuted: the "lies" that mislead them are "their (own) lies" [Calvin].<div eID="gen23045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after ... which their fathers ... walked--</hi>We are not to follow the fathers in error, but must follow the word of God alone. It was an aggravation of the Jews' sin that it was not confined to preceding generations; the sins of the sons rivalled those of their fathers (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.32">Mt 23:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>) [Calvin]. <div eID="gen23046" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b5d2b71863378122c0c3330fd1043835a60ad23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12526"/><div sID="gen23047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12526"/><hi type="bold">5. a fire--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar. <div eID="gen23047" type="x-p"/>
entries.d84a1cf76231fc6f09f4c733b54e6110b334be27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12527"/><div sID="gen23048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12527"/><hi type="bold">6. Israel--</hi>the ten tribes, the main subject of Amos' prophecies.<div eID="gen23048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sold the righteous--</hi>Israel's judges for a bribe are induced to condemn in judgment him who has a righteous cause; in violation of <reference osisRef="Deut.16.19">De 16:19</reference>.<div eID="gen23049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the poor for a pair of shoes--</hi>literally, "sandals" of wood, secured on the foot by leather straps; less valuable than shoes. Compare the same phrase, for "the most paltry bribe," <reference osisRef="Amos.8.6">Am 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.19">Eze 13:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.3">Joe 3:3</reference>. They were not driven by poverty to such a sin; beginning with suffering themselves to be tempted by a large bribe, they at last are so reckless of all shame as to prostitute justice for the merest trifle. Amos convicts them of injustice, incestuous unchastity, and oppression first, as these were so notorious that they could not deny them, before he proceeds to reprove their contempt of God, which they would have denied on the ground that they worshipped God in the form of the calves. <div eID="gen23050" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2a10a7d02a8c795d164dcd30ff33b43b5aacf40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12528"/><div sID="gen23051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12528"/><hi type="bold">7. pant after ... dust of ... earth on ... head of ... poor--</hi>that is, eagerly thirst for this object, by their oppression to prostrate the poor so as to cast the dust on their heads in mourning on the earth (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.2">2Sa 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.12">Job 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.30">Eze 27:30</reference>).<div eID="gen23051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn aside ... way of ... meek--</hi>pervert their cause (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.12">Am 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.4">Job 24:4</reference> [Grotius]; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.2">Is 10:2</reference>).<div eID="gen23052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a man and his father--</hi>a crime "not so much as named among the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.1">1Co 5:1</reference>). When God's people sin in the face of light, they often fall lower than even those who know not God.<div eID="gen23053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go in unto the same maid--</hi>from <reference osisRef="Amos.2.8">Am 2:8</reference> it seems likely "the damsel" meant is one of the prostitutes attached to the idol Astarte's temple: prostitution being part of her filthy worship.<div eID="gen23054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to profane my ... name--</hi>Israel in such abominations, as it were, designedly seeks to insult God. <div eID="gen23055" type="x-p"/>
entries.109a0e5c0ca6582858b55fb8f1ab8c10c00621c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12529"/><div sID="gen23056" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12529"/><hi type="bold">8. lay themselves ... upon clothes laid to pledge--</hi>the outer garment, which <reference osisRef="Exod.22.25-Exod.22.27">Ex 22:25-27</reference> ordered to be restored to the poor man before sunset, as being his only covering. It aggravated the crime that they lay on these clothes in an idol temple.<div eID="gen23056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by every altar--</hi>They partook in a recumbent posture of their idolatrous feasts; the ancients being in the habit of reclining at full length in eating, the upper part of the body resting on the left elbow, not sitting as we do.<div eID="gen23057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drink ... wine of the condemned--</hi>that is, wine bought with the money of those whom they unjustly fined. <div eID="gen23058" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3e28911715befd96906fea140ed5b5af667cdd0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12530"/><div sID="gen23059" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12530"/><hi type="bold">9. Yet--</hi>My former benefits to you heighten your ingratitude.<div eID="gen23059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Amorite--</hi>the most powerful of all the Canaanite nations, and therefore put for them all (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Ge 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">48:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.1.20">De 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.7.7">Jos 7:7</reference>).<div eID="gen23060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">height ... like ... cedars--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.13.32">Nu 13:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.13.33">33</reference>).<div eID="gen23061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destroyed his fruit ... above ... roots ... beneath--</hi>that is, destroyed him utterly (<reference osisRef="Job.18.16">Job 18:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.9">Eze 17:9</reference>; Mal 4:1). <div eID="gen23062" type="x-p"/>
entries.25f9c9fc9255ee36347196cb367dcde6a32abcb0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12531"/><div sID="gen23063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12531"/><hi type="bold">10. brought you up from ... Egypt--</hi>"brought up" is the phrase, as Egypt was low and flat, and Canaan hilly.<div eID="gen23063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to possess the land of the Amorite--</hi>The Amorites strictly occupied both sides of the Jordan and the mountains afterward possessed by Judah; but they here, as in <reference osisRef="Amos.2.9">Am 2:9</reference>, stand for all the Canaanites. God kept Israel forty years in the wilderness, which tended to discipline them in His statutes, so as to be the better fitted for entering on the possession of Canaan. <div eID="gen23064" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa33d8f6b91d54460277ef5a8d593b48b7b5d8f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12532"/><div sID="gen23065" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12532"/>11. Additional obligations under which Israel lay to God; the prophets and Nazarites, appointed by Him, to furnish religious instruction and examples of holy self-restraint.<div eID="gen23065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of your young men--</hi>It was a specimen of Israel's highly favored state, that, of the class most addicted to pleasures, God chose those who by a solemn vow bound themselves to abstinence from all produce of the vine, and from all ceremonial and moral defilement. The Nazarite was not to shave (<reference osisRef="Num.6.2">Nu 6:2</reference>, &c.). God left nothing undone to secure the purity of their worship and their faithfulness to it (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.7">La 4:7</reference>). The same comes from a Hebrew root, nazar, "to set apart." Samson, Samuel, and John the Baptist were Nazarites.<div eID="gen23066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Is it not even thus--</hi>Will any of you dare to deny it is so? <div eID="gen23067" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a49577b7f3b71c87fb4283d89421fa33bc47d34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12533"/><div sID="gen23068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12533"/>12. Ye so despised these My favors, as to tempt the Nazarite to break his vow; and forbade the prophets prophesying (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Is 30:10</reference>). So Amaziah forbade Amos (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.12">Am 7:12</reference>, 13, 14). <div eID="gen23068" type="x-p"/>
entries.62cb0d001d01395ae816cb7d017b469bdffb03d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12534"/><div sID="gen23069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12534"/><hi type="bold">13. I am pressed under you--</hi>so Calvin (Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.14">Is 1:14</reference>). The Margin translates actively, "I will depress your place," that is, "I will make it narrow," a metaphor for afflicting a people; the opposite of enlarging, that is, relieving (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.4.12">Pr 4:12</reference>). Maurer translates, "I will press you down" (not as Margin, "your place"; so the Hebrew, <reference osisRef="Job.40.12">Job 40:12</reference>; or <reference osisRef="Amos.2.7">Am 2:7</reference> in Hebrew text). Amos, as a shepherd, appropriately draws his similes from rustic scenes. <div eID="gen23069" type="x-p"/>
entries.62b117274b8c678bcbec13dc2565f77e331c367d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12535"/><div sID="gen23070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12535"/><hi type="bold">14. flight shall perish from ... swift--</hi>Even the swift shall not be able to escape.<div eID="gen23070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strong shall not strengthen his force--</hi>that is, shall not be able to use his strength.<div eID="gen23071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">himself--</hi>literally, "his life." <div eID="gen23072" type="x-p"/>
entries.68be3e4a5a0829d00fae5b6ed1f5adae61406f2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12536"/><div sID="gen23073" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12536"/><hi type="bold">16. flee ... naked--</hi>If any escape, it must be with the loss of accoutrements, and all that would impede rapid flight. They must be content with saving their life alone. <chapter eID="Amos.2"/>

entries.707f6413c1d0ac5c73ce86cfcb8e26da91c5b12a: <div eID="gen34249" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34250" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34251" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34251" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34250" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34252" type="x-p"/> The prophet goes on to declare the judgments of God against Moab, <reference osisRef="Amo.2.1-Amo.2.3">Amo 2:1-3</reference>; against Judah, <reference osisRef="Amo.2.4">Amo 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amo.2.5">Amo 2:5</reference>; and then against Israel, the particular object of his mission. He enumerates some of their sins, <reference osisRef="Amo.2.6-Amo.2.8">Amo 2:6-8</reference>, aggravated by God's distinguishing regard to Israel, <reference osisRef="Amo.2.9-Amo.2.12">Amo 2:9-12</reference>; and they are in consequence threatened with dreadful punishments, <reference osisRef="Amo.2.13-Amo.2.16">Amo 2:13-16</reference>. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Kgs 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Kgs 17:6</reference>. <div eID="gen34252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34253" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34254" type="x-p"/> For three transgressions of Moab and for four - See an explanation of this form <reference osisRef="Amo.1.2">Amo 1:2</reference>. The land of the Moabites lay to the east of the Dead Sea. For the origin of this people, see <reference osisRef="Gen.19.37">Gen 19:37</reference>. <div eID="gen34254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34255" type="x-p"/> He burned the bones on the king of Edom into lime - Possibly referring to some brutality; such as opening the grave of one of the Idumean kings, and calcining his bones. It is supposed by some to refer to the fact mentioned <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.26">2Kgs 3:26</reference>, when the kings of Judah, Israel, and Idumea, joined together to destroy Moab. The king of it, despairing to save his city, took seven hundred men, and made a desperate sortie on the quarter where the king of Edom was; and, though not successful, took prisoner the son of the king of Edom; and, on their return into the city, offered him as a burnt-offering upon the wall, so as to terrify the besieging armies, and cause them to raise the siege. Others understand the son that was sacrificed to be the king of Moab's own son.
entries.cea8c9f835685eeada497204739e3d78008abf12: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34256" type="x-p"/> The palaces of Kirioth - This was one of the principal cities of the Moabites. <div eID="gen34256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34257" type="x-p"/> Moab shall die with tumult - All these expressions seem to refer to this city's being taken by storm, which was followed by a total slaughter of its inhabitants.
entries.cf8ac24efb10e5f71a786152a8402e2bd3c42daa: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34258" type="x-p"/> I will cut off the judge - It shall be so destroyed, that it shall never more have any form of government. The judge here, שופט shophet, may signify the chief magistrate. The chief magistrates of the Carthaginians were called suffetes; probably taken from the Hebrew Judges, שופטים shophetim.
entries.df4f166a220e596f9e27c10ec0e6f73e653c0191: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34259" type="x-p"/> For three transgressions of Judah - We may take the three and four here to any latitude; for this people lived in continual hostility to their God, from the days of David to the time of Uzziah, under whom Amos prophesied. Their iniquities are summed up under three general heads: <div eID="gen34259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34260" type="x-p"/> 1. They despised, or rejected the law of the Lord. <div eID="gen34260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34261" type="x-p"/> 2. They kept not his statutes. <div eID="gen34261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34262" type="x-p"/> 3. They followed lies, were idolaters, and followed false prophets rather than those sent by Jehovah.
entries.b8eba28a5fdff942880979b90ac4978c3031921b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34263" type="x-p"/> I will send a fire upon Judah - This fire was the war made upon the Jews by Nebuchadnezzar, which terminated with the sackage and burning of Jerusalem and its palace the temple.
entries.6d9c20609946f7daa5fb15268b13184b40f35e35: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34264" type="x-p"/> For three transgressions of Israel, etc. - To be satisfied of the exceeding delinquency of this people, we have only to open the historical and prophetic books in any part; for the whole history of the Israelites is one tissue of transgression against God. Their crimes are enumerated under the following heads: - <div eID="gen34264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34265" type="x-p"/> 1. Their judges were mercenary and corrupt. They took bribes to condemn the righteous; and even for articles of clothing, such as a pair of shoes, they condemned the poor man, and delivered him into the hands of his adversary. <div eID="gen34265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34266" type="x-p"/> 2. They were unmerciful to the poor generally. They pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor; or, to put it on the head of the poor; or, they bruise the head of the poor against the dust of the earth. Howsoever the clause is understood, it shows them to have been general oppressors of the poor, showing them neither justice nor mercy. <div eID="gen34266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34267" type="x-p"/> 3. They turn aside the way of the meek. They are peculiarly oppressive to the weak and afflicted. <div eID="gen34267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34268" type="x-p"/> 4. They were licentious to the uttermost abomination; for in their idol feasts, where young women prostituted themselves publicly in honor of Astarte, the father and son entered into impure connections with the same female. <div eID="gen34268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34269" type="x-p"/> 5. They were cruel in their oppressions of the poor; for the garments or beds which the poor had pledged they retained contrary to the law, Exodus 22:7-26, which required that such things should be restored before the setting of the sun. <div eID="gen34269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34270" type="x-p"/> 6. They punished the people by unjust and oppressive fines, and served their tables with wine bought by such fines. Or it may be understood of their appropriating to themselves that wine which was allowed to criminals to mitigate their sufferings in the article of death; which was the excess of inhumanity and cruelty.
entries.b8c8d00e6f4efea43dadb345b32725cf7bb2ca27: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34271" type="x-p"/> Yet destroyed I the Amorite - Here follow general heads of God's mercies to them, and the great things he had done for them. <div eID="gen34271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34272" type="x-p"/> 1. Bringing them out of Egypt. <div eID="gen34272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34273" type="x-p"/> 2. Miraculously sustaining them in the wilderness forty years. <div eID="gen34273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34274" type="x-p"/> 3. Driving out the Canaanites before them, and giving them possession of the promised land. <div eID="gen34274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34275" type="x-p"/> 4. Raising up prophets among them to declare the Divine will. <div eID="gen34275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34276" type="x-p"/> 5. And forming the holy institution of the Nazarites among them, to show the spiritual nature of his holy religion, <reference osisRef="Amo.2.9-Amo.2.11">Amo 2:9-11</reference>.
entries.56973a0bd0a7515e50694519625e94f2c62d3c62: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34277" type="x-p"/> But ye gave the Nazarites wine - This was expressly forbidden in the laws of their institution. See <reference osisRef="Num.6.1-Num.6.3">Num 6:1-3</reference>. <div eID="gen34277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34278" type="x-p"/> Prophesy not - They would not worship God, and they would not hear the voice of his prophets.
entries.d121c0a03118d16c9c9f8526fd7b89f53324a473: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34279" type="x-p"/> Behold, I am pressed under you - The marginal reading is better: "Behold, I will press your place, as a cart full of sheaves presseth." I will bring over you the wheel of destruction; and it shall grind your place - your city and temple, as the wheel of a cart laden with sheaves presses down the ground, gravel, and stones over which it rolls.
entries.abb80626d14e0e167b2fe4a9a661587a2e8c20f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen34279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34280" type="x-p"/> The flight shall perish from the swift - The swiftest shall not be able to save himself from a swifter destruction. None, by might, by counsel, or by fleetness, shall be able to escape from the impending ruin. In a word, God has so fully determined to avenge the quarrel of his broken covenant, that all attempts to escape from his judgments shall be useless.
entries.f6d99fc31f4791fa1649760605d7382ccc41a9a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen34280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34281" type="x-p"/> Neither shall he that rideth the horse deliver himself - I believe all these sayings, <reference osisRef="Amo.2.13-Amo.2.16">Amo 2:13-16</reference>, are proverbs, to show the inutility of all attempts, even in the best circumstances, to escape the doom now decreed, because the cup of their iniquity was full.
entries.e4877752e201c592988126f76b162b9834ae1365: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen34281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34282" type="x-p"/> Shall flee away naked - In some cases the alarm shall be in the night; and even the most heroic shall start from his bed, and through terror not wait to put on his clothes.  <chapter eID="Amos.2"/> <div eID="gen34282" type="x-p"/>

entries.1a39c3c528c42046f5c4607696fa593200fcc2c3: <reference osisRef="Amos.2.1-Amos.2.3">Amo 2:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen16356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16357" type="x-p"/> Moab. - Amo 2:1. <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah: for three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I shall not reverse it, because it has burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime,</hi> Amo 2:2. <hi type="italic">I send fire into Moab, and it will devour the palaces of Kirioth, and Moab will perish in the tumult, in the war-cry, in the trumpet-blast.</hi> Amo 2:3. <hi type="italic">And I cut off the judge from the midst thereof, and all its princes do I strangle with it, saith Jehovah.” </hi> The burning of the bones of the king of Edom is not burning while he was still alive, but the burning of the corpse into lime, i.e., so completely that the bones turned into powder like lime (D. Kimchi), to cool his wrath still further upon the dead man (cf. 2Ki 23:16). This is the only thing blamed, not his having put him to death. No record has been preserved of this event in the historical books of the Old Testament; but it was no doubt connected with the war referred to in 2 Kings 3, which Joram of Israel and Jehoshaphat of Judah waged against the Moabites in company with the king of Edom; so that the Jewish tradition found in Jerome, viz., that after this war the Moabites dug up the bones of the king of Edom from the grace, and heaped insults upon them by burning them to ashes, is apparently not without foundation. As Amos in the case of all the other nations has mentioned only crimes that were committed against the covenant nation, the one with which the Moabites are charged must have been in some way associated with either Israel or Judah, that is to say, it must have been committed upon a king of Edom, who was a vassal of Judah, and therefore not very long after this war, since the Edomites shook off their dependence upon Judah in less than ten years from that time (2Ki 8:20). As a punishment for this, Moab was to be laid waste by the fire of war, and Keriyoth with its palaces to be burned down. הקּריּות is not an appellative noun (τῶν πόλεων αὐτῆς, lxx), but a proper name of one of the chief cities of Moab (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.48.24">Jer 48:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.41">Jer 48:41</reference>), the ruins of which have been discovered by Burckhardt (<hi type="italic">Syr</hi>. p. 630) and Seetzen (ii. p. 342, cf. iv. p. 384) in the decayed town of <hi type="italic">Kereyat</hi> or <hi type="italic">Körriât</hi>. The application of the term מת to Moab is to be explained on the supposition that the nation is personified. שׁאון signifies war tumult, and  בּתרוּעה  is explained as in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.14">Amo 1:14</reference> by  בּקול שׁופר,  blast of the trumpets, the signal for the assault or for the commencement of the battle. The judge with all the princes shall be cut off <hi type="italic">miqqirbâh</hi>, i.e., out of the land of Moab. The feminine suffix refers to Moab as a land or kingdom, and not to Keriyoth. From the fact that the <hi type="italic">shōphēt</hi> is mentioned instead of the king, it has been concluded by some that Moab had no king at that time, but had only a <hi type="italic">shōphēt</hi> as its ruler; and they have sought to account for this on the ground that Moab was at that time subject to the kingdom of the ten tribes (Hitzig and Ewald). But there is no notice in the history of anything of the kind, and it cannot possibly be inferred from the fact that Jeroboam restored the ancient boundaries of the kingdom as far as the Dead Sea (2Ki 14:25). <hi type="italic">Shōphēt</hi> is analogous to <hi type="italic">tōmēkh shēbhet</hi> in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.5">Amo 1:5</reference>, and is probably nothing more than a rhetorical expression applied to the מלך, who is so called in the threat against Ammon, and simply used for the sake of variety. The threatening prophecies concerning all the nations and kingdoms mentioned from <reference osisRef="Amos.1.6">Amo 1:6</reference> onwards were fulfilled by the Chaldeans, who conquered all these kingdoms, and carried the people themselves into captivity. For fuller remarks upon this point, see at Jeremiah 48 and Eze 25:8.
entries.3ea6120982a71f865ec3d98d384f62888f92430b: <reference osisRef="Amos.2.4-Amos.2.5">Amo 2:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen16357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16358" type="x-p"/> Judah. - Amo 2:4. <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah: For three transgressions of Judah, and for four, I shall not reverse it, because they have despised the law of Jehovah, and have not kept His ordinances, and their lies led them astray, after which their fathers walked,</hi> Amo 2:5. <hi type="italic">I send fire into Judah, and it will devour the palaces of Jerusalem.” </hi> With the announcement that the storm of the wrath of God will also burst upon Judah, Amos prepares the way for passing on to Israel, the principal object of his prophecies. In the case of Judah, he condemns its contempt of the law of its God, and also its idolatry. Toorâh is the sum and substance of all the instructions and all the commandments which Jehovah had given to His people as the rule of life. <hi type="italic">Chuqqı̄m</hi> are the separate precepts contained in the <hi type="italic">thōrâh</hi>, including not only the ceremonial commands, but the moral commandments also; for the two clauses are not only parallel, but synonymous. כּזביהם, their lies, are their idols, as we may see from the relative clause, since “walking after” (<hi type="italic">bâlakh 'achărē</hi>) is the standing expression for idolatry. Amos calls the idols <hi type="italic">lies</hi>, not only as <hi type="italic">res quae fallunt</hi> (Ges.), but as fabrications and nonentities (<hi type="italic">'ĕlı̄hı̄m</hi> and <hi type="italic">hăbhâlı̄m</hi>), having no reality in themselves, and therefore quite unable to perform what was expected of them. The “fathers” who walked after these lies were their forefathers generally, since the nation of Israel practised idolatry even in the desert (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.5.26">Amo 5:26</reference>), and was more or less addicted to it ever afterwards, with the sole exception of the times of Joshua, Samuel, David, and part of the reign of Solomon, so that even the most godly kings of Judah were unable to eradicate the worship upon the high places. The punishment threatened in consequence, namely, that Jerusalem should be reduced to ashes, was carried out by Nebuchadnezzar.
entries.66953ed12f611ea3e5f2c9d4eed0225a335eabc6: <reference osisRef="Amos.2.6-Amos.2.8">Amo 2:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen16358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16359" type="x-p"/> After this introduction, the prophet’s address turns to Israel of the ten tribes, and in precisely the same form as in the case of the nations already mentioned, announces the judgment as irrevocable. At the same time, he gives a fuller description of the sins of Israel, condemning first of all the prevailing crimes of injustice and oppression, of shameless immorality and daring contempt of God (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.6-Amos.2.8">Amo 2:6-8</reference>); and secondly, its scornful contempt of the benefits conferred by the Lord (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.9-Amos.2.12">Amo 2:9-12</reference>), and threatening inevitable trouble in consequence (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.13-Amos.2.16">Amo 2:13-16</reference>). Amo 2:6. <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah: For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I shall not reverse it, because they sell the righteous for money, and the poor for a pair of shoes.</hi> Amo 2:7. <hi type="italic">They who pant after dust of the earth upon the head of the poor, and bend the way of the meek: and a man and his father go to the same girl, to desecrate my holy name.</hi> Amo 2:8. <hi type="italic">And they stretch themselves upon pawned clothes by every altar, and they drink the wine of the punished in the house of their God.” </hi> The prophet condemns four kinds of crimes. The <hi type="italic">first</hi> is unjust treatment, or condemnation of the innocent in their administration of justice. Selling the righteous for silver, i.e., for money, refers to the judges, who were bribed to punish a man as guilty of the crime of which he was accused, when he was really <hi type="italic">tsaddı̄q</hi>, i.e., righteous in a judicial, not in a moral sense, or innocent of any punishable crime. <hi type="italic">Bakkeseph</hi>, for money, i.e., either to obtain money, or for the money which they had already received, viz., from the accuser, for condemning the innocent. בּעבוּר, on account of, is not synonymous with ב <hi type="italic">pretii</hi>; for they did not sell the poor man merely to get a pair of sandals for him, as the worst possible slave was certainly worth much more than this (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.21.32">Exo 21:32</reference>); but the poor debtor who could not pay for a pair of shoes, i.e., for the merest trifle, the judge would give up to the creditor for a salve, on the strength of the law in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Lev 25:39</reference> (cf. 2Ki 4:1). <div eID="gen16359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16360" type="x-p"/> As a <hi type="italic">second</hi> crime, Amos reproves in v. 7 <hi type="italic">a</hi> their thirst for the oppression of the quiet in the land. דּלּים, ταπεινοί, and ענוים, πραεῖς. The address is carried on in participles, in the form of lively appeal, instead of quiet description, as is frequently the case in Amos (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">Amo 5:7</reference>; Amo 6:3., 13, <reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">Amo 8:14</reference>), and also in other books (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Isa 40:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Isa 40:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.19.11">Psa 19:11</reference>). In the present instance, the article before the participle points back to the suffix in מכרם, and the finite verb is not introduced till the second clause. שׁאף, to gasp, to pant, to long eagerly for earth-dust upon the head of the poor, i.e., to long to see the head of the poor covered with earth or dust, or to bring them into such a state of misery, that they scatter dust upon their head (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.2.12">Job 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.2">2Sa 1:2</reference>). The explanation given by Hitzig is too far-fetched and unnatural, viz., that they grudge the man in distress even the handful of dust that he has strewn upon his head, and avariciously long for it themselves. To bend the way of the meek, i.e., to bring them into a trap, or cast them headlong into destruction by impediments and stumblingblocks laid in their path. The way is the way of life, their outward course. The idea that the way refers to the judgment or legal process is too contracted. The <hi type="italic">third</hi> crime is their profanation of the name of God by shameless immorality (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Amos.2.7">Amo 2:7</reference></hi>); and the <hi type="italic">fourth</hi>, desecration of the sanctuary by drinking carousals (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.8">Amo 2:8</reference>). A man and his father, i.e., both son and father, go to the girl, i.e., to the prostitute. The meaning is, to one and the same girl; but <hi type="italic">'achath</hi> is omitted, to preclude all possible misunderstanding, as though going to different prostitutes was allowed. This sin was tantamount to incest, which, according to the law, was to be punished with death (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.18.7">Lev 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.15">Lev 18:15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lev.20.11">Lev 20:11</reference>). Temple girls (<hi type="italic">qedēshōth</hi>) are not to be thought of here. The profanation of the name of God by such conduct as this does not indicate prostitution in the temple itself, such as was required by the licentious worship of Baal and Asherah (Ewald, Maurer, etc.), but consisted in a daring contempt of the commandments of God, as the original passage (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.32">Lev 22:32</reference>) from which Amos took the words clearly shows (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.34.16">Jer 34:16</reference>). By <hi type="italic">lema‛an</hi>, in order that (not “so that”), the profanation of the holy name of God is represented as intentional, to bring out the daring character of the sin, and to show that it did not arise from weakness or ignorance, but was practised with studious contempt of the holy God. <hi type="italic">Begâdı̄m chăbhulı̄m</hi>, pawned clothes, i.e., upper garments, consisting of a large square piece of cloth, which was wrapt all around, and served the poor for a counterpane as well. If a poor man was obliged to pawn his upper garment, it was to be returned to him before night came on (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.25">Exo 22:25</reference>), and a garment so pawned was not to be slept upon (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.12-Deut.24.13">Deu 24:12-13</reference>). But godless usurers kept such pledges, and used them as cloths upon which they stretched their limbs at feasts (<hi type="italic">yattū</hi>, <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>, to stretch out, sc. the body or its limbs); and this they did by every altar, at sacrificial meals, without standing in awe of God. It is very evident that Amos is speaking of sacrificial feasting, from the reference in the second clause of the verse to the drinking of wine in the house of God. עמוּשׁים, punished in money, i.e., fined. Wine of the punished is wine purchased by the produce of the fines. Here again the emphasis rests upon the fact, that such drinking carousals were held in the house of God. <hi type="italic">'Elōhēhem</hi>, not their gods (idols), but their God; for Amos had in his mind the sacred places at Bethel and Dan, in which the Israelites worshipped Jehovah as their God under the symbol of an ox (calf). The expression <hi type="italic">col</hi>-<hi type="italic">mizbēăch</hi> (every altar) is not at variance with this; for even if <hi type="italic">col</hi> pointed to a plurality of altars, these altars were still <hi type="italic">bāmōth</hi>, dedicated to Jehovah. If the prophet had also meant to condemn actual idolatry, i.e., the worship of heathen deities, he would have expressed this more clearly; to say nothing of the fact, that in the time of Jeroboam II there was no heathenish idolatry in the kingdom of the ten tribes, or, at any rate, it was not publicly maintained.
entries.011fc9ef5b3d58f2a520472cf017751aa3aff20e: <reference osisRef="Amos.2.9-Amos.2.10">Amo 2:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen16360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16361" type="x-p"/> And if this daring contempt of the commandments of God was highly reprehensible even in itself, it became perfectly inexcusable if we bear in mind that Israel was indebted to the Lord its God for its elevation into an independent nation, and also for its sacred calling. For this reason, the prophet reminds the people of the manifestations of grace which it had received from its God (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.9-Amos.2.11">Amo 2:9-11</reference>). Amo 2:9. <hi type="italic">“And yet I destroyed the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars, and who was strong as the oaks; and I destroyed his fruit from above, and his roots from beneath.</hi> Amo 2:10. <hi type="italic">And yet I brought you up from the land of Egypt, and led you forty years in the desert, to take possession of the land of the Amorite.” </hi> The repeated ואנכי is used with peculiar emphasis, and serves to bring out the contrast between the conduct of the Israelites towards the Lord, and the fidelity of the Lord towards Israel. Of the two manifestations of divine grace to which Israel owed its existence as an independent nation, Amos mentions first of all the destruction of the former inhabitants of Canaan (Exo 23:27., <reference osisRef="Exod.34.11">Exo 34:11</reference>); and secondly, what was earlier in point of time, namely, the deliverance out of Egypt and guidance through the Arabian desert; not because the former act of God was greater than the latter, but in order to place first what the Lord had done for the nation, that he may be able to append to this what He still continues to do (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.11">Amo 2:11</reference>). The nations destroyed before Israel are called Amorites, from the most powerful of the Canaanitish tribes, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Gen 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.24.15">Jos 24:15</reference>, etc. To show, however, that Israel was not able to destroy this people by its own strength, but that Jehovah the Almighty God alone could accomplish this, he proceeds to transfer to the whole nation what the Israelitish spies reported as to their size, more especially as to the size of particular giants (Num 13:32-33), and describes the Amorites as giants as lofty as trees and as strong as trees, and, continuing the same figure, depicts their utter destruction or extermination as the destruction of their fruit and of their roots. For this figure of speech, in which the posterity of a nation is regarded as its fruit, and the kernel of the nation out of which it springs as the root, see <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.9">Eze 17:9</reference>; Hos 9:16; Job 18:16. These two manifestations of divine mercy Moses impressed more than once upon the hearts of the people in his last addresses, to urge them in consequence to hold fast to the divine commandments and to the love of God (cf. Deu 8:2., <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1-Deut.9.6">Deu 9:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.1-Deut.29.8">Deu 29:1-8</reference>).
entries.f1310813a374861359e867b03712c9831fc9a03e: <reference osisRef="Amos.2.11-Amos.2.12">Amo 2:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen16361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16362" type="x-p"/> But Jehovah had not only put Israel into possession of Canaan; He had also continually manifested Himself to it as the founder and promoter of its spiritual prosperity. Amo 2:11. <hi type="italic">“And I raised up some of your sons as prophets, and some of your young men as dedicated ones (Naziraeans). Ah, is it not so, ye sons of Israel? is the saying of Jehovah. </hi> Amo 2:12. <hi type="italic">But ye made the dedicated drink wine, and ye commanded the prophets, saying, Ye shall not prophesy.” </hi> The institution of prophecy and the law of the Nazarite were gifts of grace, in which Israel had an advantage over every other nation, and by which it was distinguished above the heathen as the nation of God and the medium of salvation. Amos simply reminds the people of these, and not of earthly blessings, which the heathen also enjoyed, since the former alone were real pledges of the covenant of grace made by Jehovah with Israel; and it was in the contempt and abuse of these gifts of grace that the ingratitude of the nation was displayed in the most glaring light. The Nazarites are placed by the side of the prophets, who proclaimed to the nation the counsel and will of the Lord, because, although as a rule the condition of a Nazarite was merely the consequence of his own free will and the fulfilment of a particular vow, it was nevertheless so far a gift of grace from the Lord, that the resolution to perform such a vow proceeded from the inward impulse of the Spirit of God, and the performance itself was rendered possible through the power of this Spirit alone. (For a general discussion of the law of the Nazarite, see the commentary on Num 6:2-12, and my <hi type="italic">biblical Antiquities</hi>, §67.) The raising up of Nazarites was not only intended to set before the eyes of the people the object of their divine calling, or their appointment to be a holy nation of God, but also to show them how the Lord bestowed the power to carry out this object. But instead of suffering themselves to be spurred on by these types to strive earnestly after sanctification of life, they tempted the Nazarites to break their vow by drinking wine, from which they were commanded to abstain, as being irreconcilable with the seriousness of their sanctification (see my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Ant.</hi> §67); and the prophets they prohibited from prophesying, because the word of God was burdensome to them (cf. Amo 7:10.; Mic 2:6).
entries.96dc00287ca054dc697cf26aea71d597775076b9: <reference osisRef="Amos.2.13-Amos.2.16">Amo 2:13-16</reference> <div eID="gen16362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16363" type="x-p"/> This base contempt of their covenant mercies the Lord would visit with a severe punishment. Amo 2:13. <hi type="italic">“Behold, I will press you down, as the cart presses that is filled with sheaves.</hi> Amo 2:14. <hi type="italic">And the flight will be lost to the swift, and the strong one will not fortify his strength, and the hero will not deliver his soul.</hi> Amo 2:15. <hi type="italic">And the carrier of the bow will not stand, and the swift-footed will not deliver, and the rider of the horse will not save his soul.</hi> Amo 2:16. <hi type="italic">And the courageous one among the heroes will flee away naked in that day, is the saying of Jehovah.” </hi> The Lord threatens as a punishment a severe oppression, which no one will be able to escape. The allusion is to the force of war, under which even the bravest and most able heroes will succumb. העיק, from עוּק, Aramaean for צוּק, to press, construed with <hi type="italic">tachath</hi>, in the sense of κατὰ, downwards, to press down upon a person, i.e., to press him down (Winer, Ges., Ewald). This meaning is established by עקה in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.4">Psa 55:4</reference>, and by מוּעקה in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.11">Psa 66:11</reference>; so that there is no necessity to resort to the Arabic, as Hitzig does, or to alterations of the text, or to follow Baur, who gives the word the meaning, “to feel one’s self pressed under another,” for which there is no foundation in the language, and which does not even yield a suitable sense.
